title: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two stacks. Also discuss implementing a stack using two queues.
shortTitle: Implement Queue using two Stacks / Stack using two Queues
keyPoints: Two stacks make a queue: push to inbox, pour inbox into outbox only when outbox is empty, then pop outbox.
Lazy transfer gives amortized O(1) per operation because each element moves between stacks at most once.
Eager transfer on every dequeue destroys both the ordering and the amortized guarantee.
A stack from one queue: on push, add the element then rotate all earlier elements behind it, making push O(n) and pop O(1).
The two-stack queue is practically useful; the queue-based stack is mostly an interview exercise.
This pattern underpins the Banker's queue in functional data structures where two lists replace the two stacks.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use an inbox stack for pushes and an outbox stack for pops; flip the inbox into the outbox only when the outbox is empty for amortized O(1).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Queue from two stacks** – simulate FIFO with two LIFO stacks by pushing to an inbox and transferring to an outbox only when the outbox is empty, reversing the order so the oldest element is on top.
- **Amortized O(1)** – each element is pushed to inbox once, transferred to outbox once, and popped once, so the cost per element is constant over its lifetime.
- **Stack from one queue** – simulate LIFO by rotating the queue on every push so the newest element sits at the front, making push O(n) and pop O(1).
- **Lazy transfer rule** – transfer only when the outbox is empty; eager transfer on every operation breaks ordering and complexity.
- **Practical relevance** – the two-stack queue appears in functional data structures (Banker's queue) and constrained environments where only stacks are available.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh processes customer cheques at National Bank of India, but he only has two in-trays that behave like stacks. Customers must be served in arrival order. He drops every new cheque into the incoming tray. When he needs to serve the next customer, if the serving tray is empty he flips the whole incoming tray onto the serving tray one by one, which reverses the order so the oldest cheque is on top. He serves from the serving tray until it empties, then flips again only when needed.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Two-Stack Queue Operation
  ─────────────────────────

  enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C):

  Inbox          Outbox
  ┌─────┐        ┌─────┐
  │  C  │ top    │     │ empty
  ├─────┤        └─────┘
  │  B  │
  ├─────┤
  │  A  │
  └─────┘

  dequeue() → outbox empty, transfer:

  Inbox          Outbox
  ┌─────┐        ┌─────┐
  │     │ empty  │  A  │ top  ← oldest on top!
  └─────┘        ├─────┤
                 │  B  │
                 ├─────┤
                 │  C  │
                 └─────┘

  pop outbox → returns A (FIFO order)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Implementing a queue with two stacks is a lesson in how reversing order with one structure gives you the behavior of its opposite. I keep an inbox stack and an outbox stack. Every enqueue pushes onto the inbox in O(1). Every dequeue serves from the outbox, and only when the outbox is empty do I pour the entire inbox into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top.

The lazy transfer rule is what makes this efficient. Each element moves from inbox to outbox exactly once in its lifetime, so the amortized cost per operation is O(1) even though one particular dequeue that triggers a transfer can be O(n). Transferring on every dequeue would break both the ordering and the complexity guarantee.

The mirror problem of building a stack from a queue has no amortized constant-time solution for both operations. The common approach rotates a single queue on every push so the newest element sits at the front, making push O(n) and pop O(1). It is a fine interview exercise but far less practical than the two-stack queue.

In my project at the National Bank of India, I used this in a cheque-clearing module where the legacy buffers behaved like stacks but cheques had to be processed in arrival order. The inbox collected arrivals and the outbox served them in corrected order, and the lazy-flip rule kept throughput high during burst clearing.

Remember one sentence: push to inbox, pour into outbox only when it is empty, and each element moves at most once for amortized O(1).
